103	$\pi_0.5$ shows moderate complexity amplification under L2 norm pruning at $k{=}0.95$: Object retains 98.2\% (matching the baseline), Spatial retains 97.8\% (within noise of the 97.2\% baseline), and Goal drops to 89.4\% ($-$7.0\,pp from 96.4\%). Simple tasks absorb mild pruning with negligible loss; compositional tasks expose measurable degradation even at 5\% token removal.
104	
105	X-VLA exhibits dramatic complexity amplification. At $k{=}0.9$ with L2 norm selection, Object retains the full 99.2\% baseline, while Goal drops to 70.2\% ($-$27.8\,pp). Object absorbs 10\% token removal with zero loss; the same pruning ratio on multi-step tasks produces near-catastrophic degradation, driven entirely by task complexity with the same model and pruning method. The effect is even more pronounced at $k{=}0.95$ on Long: removing just 3 of 50 tokens collapses SR from 94.0\% to 47.0\%, a 47.0\,pp loss, while Object at the same ratio loses only 0.2\,pp.
106	
107	Token-entangling connectors (X-VLA's BART encoder) amplify task complexity because compositional tasks require integrating information across spatial locations. When the BART encoder creates cross-token dependencies, removing even a few tokens disrupts the distributed representations that multi-step tasks rely on. Token-independent connectors ($\pi_0.5$'s linear projection, OpenVLA's MLP) show moderate complexity amplification because each token's contribution is self-contained: removing tokens reduces spatial coverage proportionally, and simple tasks tolerate the resulting gaps.

\subsection{VTR Recovery}
\label{sec:vtr_recovery}

Vision Token Re-encoder (VTR) addresses the catastrophic cliff through learned re-encoding rather than hard deletion. VTR inserts a lightweight cross-attention module ($\sim$22M parameters, approximately 5\% of SmolVLA) between the pixel-shuffle connector and the LLM backbone. $M$ learned queries attend over the full set of 128 source tokens and produce $M$ compressed output representations, where $M \in \{16, 32, 64, 96, 128\}$. The $M{=}128$ configuration serves as a passthrough control that re-encodes without compressing.

Table~\ref{tab:vtr_results} reports VTR results on SmolVLA for LIBERO-Object (3 seeds, 500 episodes each). Cross-attention VTR recovers substantial performance where hard pruning yields 0.0\%: $M{=}16$ (87.5\% compression) achieves 56.9 $\pm$ 1.3\%, $M{=}32$ (75\%) achieves 60.1 $\pm$ 1.3\%, $M{=}64$ (50\%) achieves 62.0 $\pm$ 2.2\%, $M{=}96$ (25\%) achieves 54.5 $\pm$ 3.2\%, and $M{=}128$ (0\%, passthrough) achieves 58.0 $\pm$ 3.5\%. The SmolVLA-Base (LoRA fine-tuned) baseline without VTR is 44.8\%, and the official SmolVLA baseline is 59.2\%.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{VTR re-encoding on SmolVLA (LIBERO-Object). Cross-attention and MLP adapter results report mean $\pm$ std over 3 seeds (500 episodes each). The M-curve is flat: $M{=}16$ (87.5\% compression) matches $M{=}128$ (passthrough) within 1.1\,pp. The baseline control (100K extra training, no compressor) confirms the gain is architectural. ``Compression'' = fraction of tokens removed.}
\label{tab:vtr_results}
\begin{tabular}{lccr}
\toprule
Configuration & $M$ & Compression & SR (\%) \\
\midrule
\textit{SmolVLA-Base (LoRA)} & 128 & 0\% & 44.8 \\
\textit{SmolVLA official} & 128 & 0\% & 59.2 \\
\textit{Baseline control (+100K steps)} & 128 & 0\% & 45.0 \\
\textit{Hard pruning (any $k$)} & -- & 5--50\% & 0.0 \\
\midrule
Cross-attn VTR & 16 & 87.5\% & 56.9 $\pm$ 1.3 \\
Cross-attn VTR & 32 & 75\% & 60.1 $\pm$ 1.3 \\
Cross-attn VTR & 64 & 50\% & \textbf{62.0 $\pm$ 2.2} \\
Cross-attn VTR & 96 & 25\% & 54.5 $\pm$ 3.2 \\
Cross-attn VTR & 128 & 0\% & 58.0 $\pm$ 3.5 \\
\midrule
MLP adapter ($\sim$22M) & 32 & 75\% & 63.4 $\pm$ 2.6 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The M-curve is notably flat: performance at $M{=}16$ (56.9\%) falls within 1.1\,pp of $M{=}128$ (58.0\%), and all five $M$ values cluster within a 7.5\,pp range. This flatness confirms that the operative factor is learned re-encoding of spatially entangled tokens, not the compression ratio itself. The VTR module transforms pixel-shuffle representations into a format the downstream LLM can process robustly, and this transformation is effective regardless of how many output tokens carry the result.

A parameter-matched MLP adapter ($\sim$22M parameters) achieves 63.4 $\pm$ 2.6\% at $M{=}32$, comparable to cross-attention VTR ($p = 0.15$). This confirms that re-encoding itself, rather than the specific attention mechanism, is the key architectural intervention. The baseline control (100K additional training steps without the compressor module) achieves only 45.0\% SR, within 0.2\,pp of the 44.8\% baseline. The performance gain is therefore attributable to the VTR architecture, not to additional optimization.

Cross-suite evaluation at $M{=}32$ confirms that VTR recovery generalizes beyond Object: Spatial achieves 53.2\% and Goal achieves 56.4\%, both recovered from 0.0\% under hard pruning.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	\paragraph{ViT token pruning and merging.}
5	Token reduction methods for Vision Transformers consistently remove 50--66\% of tokens with less than 0.5 percentage points of ImageNet accuracy loss.
6	DynamicViT~\cite{rao2021dynamicvit} learns binary masks to identify uninformative tokens,
7	EViT~\cite{liang2022evit} uses attention scores to fuse or discard low-salience patches,

269	The random cliff on $\pi_0.5$ Object (Section~\ref{sec:cross_suite}) can be modeled as a hypergeometric sampling problem. Among $N{=}768$ vision tokens, $C{=}91$ are critical. $C$ and $T$ are jointly fit by minimizing RMSE against four cliff-zone data points ($k \in \{0.85, 0.9, 0.925, 0.95\}$). When $\lfloor N(1{-}k) \rfloor$ tokens are removed uniformly at random, the number of critical tokens removed follows a hypergeometric distribution $\mathrm{Hypergeometric}(N, C, \lfloor N(1{-}k) \rfloor)$. We define performance collapse as removing $\geq T{=}6$ critical tokens simultaneously; the fit yields $C{=}91$, $T{=}6$ with RMSE${=}$0.025. The fitted $C{=}91$ (11.8\% of tokens) is broadly consistent with the top-importance center region identified in the token heatmap (Figure~\ref{fig:token_heatmap}), providing post-hoc interpretability: the ``critical tokens'' correspond to spatially concentrated, high-norm positions encoding the robot arm and target object.
270	
271	The model predicts three characteristic retention ratios: $k{=}0.963$ where $P(\text{collapse}){=}10\%$ (cliff onset), $k{=}0.937$ where $P(\text{collapse}){=}50\%$ (midpoint), and $k{=}0.902$ where $P(\text{collapse}){=}90\%$ (near-complete collapse). The cliff width $\Delta k \approx 0.06$ between 10\% and 90\% collapse probability matches the observed transition from 69.4\% SR ($k{=}0.95$) to 12.0\% SR ($k{=}0.90$). The model captures the cliff onset and sharpness but does not explain the V-shape recovery at $k \leq 0.7$, where success rate rebounds to 77.2\%. The recovery lies outside the model's scope (which assumes monotonic collapse probability). We hypothesize that at aggressive pruning the model transitions to a qualitatively different computation regime---potentially relying on coarser spatial features that survive uniform subsampling---but this remains untested.
